content.text: With hydration, the browser doesn't throw the server's HTML away. Angular runs your components again, but where it would create DOM nodes it finds the ones the server already sent, reuses them and attaches event listeners. That contract only holds while the server and the browser produce the same DOM, and code that edits the DOM behind Angular's back breaks it.

A store turns on server-side rendering, and the product page now paints almost instantly. Then the dev console shows NG0500, a hydration node mismatch, pointing at the price component. It adds a "Sale" badge in

on the root component to silence the error, and it works: no more NG0500. But now the page flickers once as it finishes loading, because that attribute brought back exactly what the team thought SSR always did: rebuild the page from scratch.

The belief: with SSR, the server sends HTML so the user sees something fast, and then the browser throws that HTML away and renders the app again. The server only buys the first paint and the SEO, and what the browser does afterwards is the same as in a client-only app.
There's real evidence for it. The browser still downloads the app's JavaScript and runs every component: a

in a constructor shows up once in the server's terminal and again in the browser console. And the belief describes a real mode of Angular SSR. The hydration guide says that without hydration enabled, a server-rendered Angular app "will destroy and re-render the application's DOM", which may cause a visible flicker. So the half-truth is this: your component code runs twice, but the DOM doesn't have to be built twice.
The server sends HTML and a map of it

On the server, Angular renders the page to HTML and annotates it. The NG0500 page describes the browser expecting the DOM structure "as rendered and annotated during server-side rendering". Part of that map lives in the markup itself: Angular's comment nodes act as anchors for view containers such as
blocks. The page can also carry data, like
responses the server already fetched, so the browser doesn't have to ask again.
The browser runs your components but adopts the DOM
When the JavaScript arrives, the app bootstraps as usual. Components are created, constructors and

run, signals and inputs get their values. The difference is in the step that would normally create elements. In the guide's words, Angular "tries to match existing DOM elements to the application's structure at runtime and reuses DOM nodes when possible". It claims the server's
instead of making a new one, and attaches listeners to it. After hydration, a cleanup step removes the nodes nobody claimed.
: the same work as a client render, minus building the DOM. The content the user is already looking at stays in place: nothing is torn down and rebuilt, so nothing flickers.
Until then, the page is a picture
Server HTML looks interactive before it is. The guide is explicit that event listeners aren't attached until hydration completes. That's what
covers: it records native events such as clicks during that window and replays them once hydration finishes. In Angular 22, event replay comes with incremental hydration, which
enables by default, so an early click on "Add to cart" isn't lost.
The contract: the same DOM on both sides
Reuse works only if the browser finds exactly what the server annotated, down to whitespace and comment nodes. The guide lists the usual ways to break that:

content.text: The fix isn't a hydration trick; it's moving the badge to where Angular can see it. In the template, the server renders the
branch, the browser reaches the same branch with the same inputs, and hydration claims the
like any other node. When you truly need imperative DOM work, such as a chart library, run it in

ngSkipHydration brings the old behavior back

on a component's host makes Angular skip hydrating that component and all its children. The guide says such a component "will destroy and re-render itself", and that putting it on the root component effectively disables hydration for the whole app. It's a last-resort workaround, and the guide treats components that need it as bugs to fix.

content.text: In development, the browser console prints hydration stats, such as how many components and nodes were hydrated. Angular DevTools can also overlay the page to show which parts were hydrated and highlight a component that caused a mismatch.

blocks.title: NG0500 only in production? Check your CDN

content.text: Hydration expects Angular's comment nodes at their original places. If a CDN or an HTML minifier strips comments from the server response, the app hydrates in development and fails in production. Turn the comment removal off.

items.title: Treat every ngSkipHydration as a bug

content.text: List each use, note the component it hides, and remove it once that component stops editing the DOM. Never put it on the root component.
